# Contributing to modern-yolonas

Thanks for your interest in contributing.

## Code of Conduct

Please read and follow the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## What this project is

modern-yolonas is a faithful, readable reimplementation of YOLO-NAS: the model, a
training loop, an inference path, and export targets. It is deliberately small. The
value is that you can read the whole thing.

## API design principles

These are the criteria a change is reviewed against. They exist because the project's
selling point is legibility — every abstraction has to earn its place.

1. **No indirection that only exists to be configurable.** No factory functions, no
   registries, no OmegaConf, no config-driven class lookup. A model variant is a
   function (`yolo_nas_s()`); a config is a dataclass. If you need to know which class
   a string maps to, you should be able to find it with grep.

2. **`state_dict` parity with super-gradients is a hard constraint.** Pretrained
   COCO checkpoints must load with `strict=True`. This pins attribute names
   (`branch_3x3.conv`, `rbr_reparam`, `post_bn`, `neck1`–`neck4`, `head1`–`head3`)
   even where a different name would read better. A change that renames a
   parameter-carrying attribute must come with a weight-remapping path and a test that
   loads a real checkpoint. `examples/parity_check.py` is the regression gate.

3. **Two layers, and they stay separate.** `YoloNAS` is a plain `nn.Module`: tensors
   in, tensors out, no file I/O, no numpy, no resizing. `Detector` is the ergonomic
   layer: paths and arrays in, decoded results out. Don't push convenience down into
   the module, and don't push tensor work up into the detector.

4. **This project detects; it does not become a computer vision toolkit.** Tracking,
   zone counting, line crossing, dataset visualisation dashboards, and annotation
   styling belong in a model-agnostic library such as
   [supervision](https://github.com/roboflow/supervision). Prefer interoperating with
   those over reimplementing them here.

5. **Inference must not pay for training.** Anything only a training run needs
   (augmentation, metrics, dataset loaders) belongs behind an optional extra or a
   function-local import, never at module import time.

6. **Numbers in the docs are reproducible or labelled as someone else's.** Every
   benchmark in `docs/benchmarks/` is generated by a script in `examples/`. Figures
   this project has not measured — such as Deci's published mAP — are marked as such.

## Development setup

```bash
uv sync --dev
uv run pre-commit install
```

## Before you open a pull request

```bash
uv run ruff check src/ tests/
uv run pytest tests/ -v
```

Tests that need model weights or heavy computation are marked `slow`; run
`uv run pytest -m "not slow"` for a quick loop.

## Branches and commits

**Branch off `dev`**, with a prefixed name: `feat/`, `fix/`, `docs/`, `chore/`, `test/`,
or `refactor/` (e.g. `fix/inference-channel-order`). Open the pull request against `dev`.

`dev` is where work lands; `main` is what has been released. Both are protected — neither
takes a direct push, and CI has to pass before a merge. `main` additionally accepts pull
requests **only from `dev`**, enforced by the `PR source guard` check, so everything on
`main` has already been integrated and tested together on `dev`.

Use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) for commit and PR
titles — `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `perf:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`, `ci:`,
`build:`, `style:`, `revert:`. Mark a breaking change with `!` (`feat!:`).

This is checked in three places, because each catches a different thing:

- **`commitizen`, as a `commit-msg` pre-commit hook** — rejects a bad message while you
  are writing it. `uv run pre-commit install` wires it up; the config sets
  `default_install_hook_types`, so the plain `install` is enough.
- **`pr-title.yml`** — validates the *pull request title*. This is the one that matters
  for history: a squash merge takes its subject from the PR title, not from your commits.
- **release-drafter** — resolves the version bump from the title directly. `feat:` and
  any `!` give `minor`; everything else gives `patch`. Something has to: before this,
  nothing set the labels the resolver read, so every release drafted as a patch — which
  is how `v0.4.0`, a `feat!`, drafted as one. The autolabeler still runs, but only to
  apply descriptive labels for filtering, so a wrong one costs a mislabelled row rather
  than a wrong release number.

The release notes are drafted from PR titles, so the title is what users will read.

## Releases

Releases are cut by merging `dev` into `main` and tagging. They are deliberate, not
automatic on every merge. Pushing a `v*` tag triggers
`publish.yml`, which builds and publishes to PyPI via trusted publishing. Pick the
version by what changed: at `0.x`, a breaking change is a minor bump, and `major` stays
unused until there is a stability contract to break. When that day comes, change the
`semver-increment` on the `breaking: true` rule in `.github/release-drafter.yml`.

The `dev` -> `main` release pull request is the exception: its title is `chore: ...`
(`pr-title.yml` rejects `release:`), which resolves to a patch, so **label it
`release:minor` (or `release:major`) by hand before merging** when the release carries
features. A label can only raise the bump, never lower it — the highest matching
increment wins.

The labels are namespaced on purpose. Dependabot puts a bare `major`/`minor`/`patch`
label on its own pull requests whenever the repository has one, describing the
*dependency* bump, and the resolver would read it as a bump of this package. Do not
recreate those bare labels.

## Supported Python versions

`requires-python` is `>=3.10`, and CI runs both ends of that range. Ruff is configured
with `target-version = "py310"` — if you need syntax newer than that, the floor moves
first, in its own pull request.
